title: Andrew Kim Taegon and companions (20 September)
hook: Korea's first native priest and 102 companions

segments.voice: Yesterday, Januarius, and a city waiting in its cathedral. Your line was the people wait.

A few books, carried home from China. That's where the Catholic story in Korea begins, as Korean Catholics tell it: not with missionaries stepping off a ship, but with Korean scholars reading Christian books, arguing over them, and wanting more. One of them traveled to Beijing, was baptized there, and came home and baptized his friends. A Church started by its own people, before any priest had come to them. Then the faith was forbidden, and the hunting began. Today, its martyrs: a priest, a layman, and their companions.
screen: `A FEW BOOKS FROM CHINA.` → `SCHOLARS WHO BAPTIZED EACH OTHER.` → `THEN THE FAITH WAS FORBIDDEN.`

segments.voice: Start with Andrew Kim Taegon. He grew up in a Catholic family when being Catholic in Korea could cost your life, and it cost his father's. As a young man he was sent abroad to study for the priesthood, and he was ordained a priest far from home. Then came his choice. He could have stayed where it was safe. Instead he slipped back into Korea in secret, to say Mass, hear confessions, and find a way to bring more priests in. He served only a short time before he was caught. He was tortured, tried, and beheaded near Seoul, still a young man. Tradition keeps a farewell letter he wrote to his people, urging them to hold together in love and not be shaken. Next, Paul Chong Hasang, a layman. His father, too, had died for the faith. He spent his life trying to bring priests to Korea, and he wrote a defense of the faith addressed to the government. He was killed as well. And then the companions: men and women, nobles and servants, catechists, mothers, young people. The Church keeps them together on one day, priest and layman, noble and servant. Jesus says in the Douay-Rheims: "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die, itself remaineth alone. But if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Some Korean Catholics read their own story in that verse: a Church begun by laypeople reading books, and planted in the ground by martyrs.
screen: `A PRIEST WHO WENT HOME IN SECRET.` · `A LAYMAN WHO WROTE IN DEFENSE.` · `NOBLES AND SERVANTS, ONE CHURCH.` · `THE GRAIN OF WHEAT.` · then, large: `IT BRINGETH FORTH MUCH FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Rest one open hand in your lap, as if a single grain of wheat lay in it, and let it stand for the people of Korea, north and south, families divided by the border, and anyone who can't practice their faith in the open. With each out-breath, let the grain go into the ground, a wish for good to grow there. If you pray, ask Saint Andrew Kim and his companions to pray for Korea; if you don't, simply wish its people peace.
Kim Taegon, baptized Andrew: the Korean priest who went home in secret to serve his people, with the layman Paul Chong Hasang and the men and women who died with them.
Your line: korea's martyrs. A Church its own people planted. That's day one thousand twenty-six.

howItsDone: On 20 September Catholics keep the memorial of Saints Andrew Kim Taegon, priest, Paul Chong Hasang, and companions, martyrs; Korean Catholic communities keep it as a great day of their own.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'Korea's first native priest' (a superlative) and '102 companions' (a count) are not stated; the script calls him a priest born in Korea and ordained abroad, and speaks of 'companions'. Confirm.
The lay origin of the Korean Church (scholars reading books from China; Yi Seung-hun baptized in Beijing, who baptized others) is given 'as Korean Catholics tell it'; Yi is not named. Confirm.

Andrew Kim: father (Ignatius Kim) martyred; ordained in Shanghai; executed at Saenamteo near Seoul, 1846, aged about 25. Dates, places and age left out. Confirm 'beheaded near Seoul, still a young man'.

Paul Chong Hasang: father (Augustine Chong Yak-jong) martyred; his letter to the government (Sang-jae-sang-seo) addressed to a minister. Script says 'addressed to the government' and screen says 'wrote to the king's men'. Confirm.
Andrew Kim's farewell letter is paraphrased only. Confirm the summary.
'Some Korean Catholics read their own story in that verse': a 'many/often' claim about a community; soften or cut if a Keeper prefers.
Practice mentions 'families divided by the border'. Confirm the tone.
